verdicts.text: In both Pulumi ESC and Vault, secrets can be stored and accessed through a CLI, SDK, or editor interface, and granular access controls can be implemented across all secrets.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC side checks out: there's a CLI (`pulumi env`), a public SDK repo (pulumi/esc-sdk), and a Pulumi Cloud document editor, and the page's own table lists access controls for both products. The Vault side (the `vault` CLI, client libraries, a web UI, and ACL policies) is widely known, but I didn't confirm it against a HashiCorp source in this session.
verdicts.source: gh search repos esc-sdk --owner pulumi; repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L66-81, L147-149
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Across all secrets" is broad marketing wording. Both products do support fine-grained policies or RBAC.

verdicts.text: Vault is not open source; it uses the Business Source License model, whereas Pulumi ESC is fully open source and Apache 2.0 licensed.
verdicts.evidence: The Apache 2.0 part holds: `gh api repos/pulumi/esc` reports license "Apache-2.0". But that repo is the ESC evaluator/CLI/SDK, and the same page calls ESC a "Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud". That hosted service isn't open source, so "fully open source" says more than the evidence supports. For Vault, GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION/"Other", which fits BSL 1.1 but doesn't prove the exact license name.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc; gh api repos/hashicorp/vault/license; repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim — the source shows 'pulumi/esc repo is Apache-2.0'; the claim says 'ESC is fully open source' about a product delivered as the Pulumi Cloud SaaS service
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Fully open source" is a risky thing to say about a product the same table describes as a fully managed SaaS service.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Each environment can be composed from multiple environments." It also lists "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration."

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can reference secrets stored in Vault, and those secrets can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC `vault-secrets` provider (`data/esc_schemas.json`: "dynamically imports Secrets from HashiCorp Vault into your Environment") backs the Vault-referencing part. Environments have revisions and tags, can import other environments, and can be cloned. The auto-generated CLI page says `pulumi env clone` will "Clone an existing environment into a new environment" and has a --preserve-history flag. So "versioned" and "composed" are clearly backed. "Branched" is a loose word for cloning: ESC has no git-style branches.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Branched" overstates things: ESC has clone/fork, not real branching with merges. Consider "forked" or "cloned".

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is Apache License 2.0 licensed; Vault is under Business Source License 1.1.
verdicts.evidence: GitHub reports pulumi/esc's license as "Apache-2.0". The hashicorp/vault LICENSE file says "Business Source License 1.1" and "Licensed Work: Vault Version 1.15.0 or later". Vault versions before 1.15 were under MPL 2.0.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc/license; gh api repos/hashicorp/vault/contents/LICENSE
verdicts.framing_note: BSL 1.1 applies only to Vault 1.15.0 and later, which is the current line. Older versions were MPL 2.0.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is a fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud; Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting requires significant management overhead.
verdicts.evidence: ESC is offered as part of the Pulumi Cloud SaaS, and Vault really does offer both a hosted service (HCP Vault) and self-hosting. One caveat: the pricing page says "we offer a self-hosted Pulumi Cloud... This option is available in the Enterprise edition." So ESC is not only available as SaaS, which the Vault row makes it look like it is. The "significant management overhead" wording is a subjective marketing comparison.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The comparison says Vault can be self-hosted but leaves out that Pulumi Cloud (and so ESC) can be self-hosted on the Enterprise edition. "Significant management overhead" is opinion, not a checkable fact.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports pulling and using secrets from multiple sources including HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager, etc.; Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC docs index lists secrets providers that let ESC "pull and synchronize secrets and configuration data, including AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, and 1Password", with provider pages under /docs/esc/providers/secrets/. That supports the ESC half. The Vault half is a competitive statement about a third-party product, and I did not check it against HashiCorp documentation.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault" oversimplifies Vault: its secrets engines issue dynamic credentials for AWS, databases and other systems. It just doesn't federate other secret stores like 1Password the way ESC does.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports both a GUI and a Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover, and error checking; Vault's editing is limited, offering a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's tutorial confirms Vault's UI has a key/value form plus a JSON toggle: "Instead of entering the key-value pairs one by one, you can enter the secret values using JSON." Pulumi's ESC editor announcement lists auto-complete, "Hover Documentation," and as-you-type error diagnostics. Calling Vault's editing "limited" is a subjective judgment, not something the sources state.
verdicts.framing_note: The ESC half is backed only by a Pulumi blog from the same site, which corroborates it but isn't independent. I found no evidence for the "GUI + Document Editor" two-mode wording itself.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI and supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference lists `pulumi env` ("Manage environments") with subcommands including "pulumi env run - Open the environment with the given name and run a command." (this is how secrets get injected as environment variables) and "pulumi env set - Set a value within an environment." / "pulumi env edit" (for modifying secrets).

verdicts.text: Vault Agent's process supervisor mode can inject secrets as environment variables (covers that use case separately).
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's official docs say: "Vault Agent's Process Supervisor Mode allows Vault secrets to be injected into a process via environment variables using Consul Template markup." The docs also describe it as a separate mode that "is incompatible with regular file template entries."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim's note that this mode covers env-var injection "separately" matches the docs. Process supervisor mode needs env_template and exec blocks and cannot be used with file templates.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault have client SDKs.
verdicts.evidence: The public repo pulumi/esc-sdk exists and holds Pulumi ESC's client SDKs. HashiCorp Vault's official client libraries (for example, the Go API client) are well known, but I couldn't check them with pulumi-scoped tools.
verdicts.source: gh search repos esc-sdk --owner pulumi → pulumi/esc-sdk (public)

verdicts.text: The Pulumi Service Provider allows management (create, update, delete) of ESC collections of secrets and configuration as a resource; Vault individual secrets can be managed with the Vault provider for Pulumi or Terraform.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/pulumi-pulumiservice repo ships Environment resource examples in every language (ts-environments, py-environments, go-environments, yaml-environments, cs-environments), so ESC environments can be managed as resources. Pulumi (pulumi/pulumi-vault) and Terraform both publish Vault providers for managing individual secrets. I didn't query pulumi-vault in this session.

verdicts.text: Vault versioning is limited; secrets are individually versioned.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's KV v2 API docs describe versioning per key ("max_versions (int: 0) – The number of versions to keep per key"), which supports "individually versioned." Only the KV v2 engine has versioning at all: KV v1 has none, and by default KV v2 keeps just 10 versions. That supports "limited," though "limited" is a comparative judgment rather than a checkable fact.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Limited" is subjective. It's accurate for KV v1 and for dynamic secrets, but KV v2 gives full per-secret version history with rollback, undelete and check-and-set writes.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC values can be secret or plaintext, whereas Vault values can only be secrets.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) ESC docs show plaintext and secret values side by side: "Any value wrapped in fn::secret is encrypted at rest and masked in output" (e.g. `region: us-west-2 # plaintext configuration`). Vault's KV engine "is used to store arbitrary secrets", and values are always encrypted ("only the values set on keys are"). There is no separate plaintext value type, so the "only secrets" wording fits, though Vault docs never say that in so many words.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim cites no source. The Vault half is inferred from Vault docs that describe all KV data as secrets whose values are encrypted. No page directly says Vault "can only" store secrets.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC lets users see existing secrets, whereas Vault does not.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs describe how to read and view existing secret values in Vault from the CLI, the API, and the UI. The kv v2 read-data page says to "Click the eye icon to view the desired key value," and the kv get page says the command "retrieves the value from KV secrets engine at the given key name." So the claim that Vault doesn't let users see existing secrets is wrong as written.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The comparison table row may mean something narrower (for example, finding secrets that already live in other stores, or ESC's own secret display), but the wording as published says Vault can't show existing secrets, which is false.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, environments can import secrets from another environment and updated secrets propagate automatically to downstream environments; Vault has no equivalent concept and has no first-class environment to reference, so secrets are read by path.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) ESC docs say "Pulumi ESC allows you to compose environments by importing configuration and secrets from other environments." Imports are resolved when an environment is opened and follow @latest by default, so updates reach downstream environments unless an import is pinned. Vault's docs say the read command "reads data from Vault at the given path", which confirms path-based access. The claim that Vault has no equivalent to environments is a negative I can't prove directly, but I found nothing contradicting it.
verdicts.framing_note: "Propagate automatically" is only true for unpinned (@latest) imports. Pinned imports (@tag or @revision) stop changes from propagating.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim says "Vault has no equivalent concept", but Vault namespaces, mounts, and policies give some structure. Also, the blanket "propagate automatically" ignores import pinning.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports constructing new dynamic values through string interpolation; Vault does not support interpolating values from other values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The KV docs I found say nothing about interpolation. A HashiCorp Discuss thread asks whether KV keys can reference each other ("wondering if it supports referencing another key within the same secret"), but the snippet doesn't include an authoritative answer. The ESC half (string interpolation) describes Pulumi's own product and needs a check against product source.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "HashiCorp Vault KV secret reference another secret interpolation"; https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/can-kv-secret-engine-keys-reference-another-key-single-source-value/77211; https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/kv/kv-v1
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Vault does not support interpolating values" is too absolute: Vault Agent/Proxy templating (consul-template) can build strings from several secrets on the client side. Only Vault's storage lacks cross-value references.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be forked for testing/branching; Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC half checks out. pulumi/esc ships `cmd/esc/cli/env_clone.go`, which lets you copy an existing environment, and ESC imports let you override specific values. The docs call this "forking", but the CLI command is `clone`. I didn't check the Vault half ("no branching or personal configs") against HashiCorp sources. It's a plausible competitive claim, since Vault offers KV versioning and namespaces but no environment branching.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Forked" loosely describes what the CLI calls clone; the claim that Vault has no branching wasn't checked against HashiCorp docs.

verdicts.text: `pulumi env diff` shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment; Vault cannot compare secrets across environments.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference says `pulumi env diff` "displays the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment," which matches the ESC half word for word. The Vault half (no way to compare secrets across environments) is a negative claim about a competitor that Pulumi sources can't check. Vault's `vault kv` has versioning but, as far as I know, no built-in diff; that is from memory, not something I checked here.
verdicts.framing_note: ESC half matches the CLI help exactly; the Vault 'No' is not confirmed.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A flat 'No' for Vault may be too strong: a user could fetch KV v2 versions and diff them by hand, so 'no built-in diff' is safer wording.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports built-in functions like `toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `fromBase64`, and `toString`.
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't confirm this from a source. GitHub code search hit its rate limit, the pulumi/esc files I could reach (the listing of the `ast` directory and the portion of `ast/expr.go` I read) don't include the builtin function table, and the local ESC builtin-function doc paths I tried don't exist. The claim's own row (vault.md L130) lists `toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `fromBase64` and `toString`, but the page under review can't count as evidence for itself.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc/contents/ast; gh search code --repo pulumi/esc fn::fromJSON (HTTP 403 rate limit)
verdicts.intuition_flag: From memory (not checked this session), ESC has fn::toJSON, fn::fromJSON, fn::fromBase64 and fn::toString, so the claim is probably true. The builtin table in the pulumi/esc eval package should settle it once the rate limit resets.

verdicts.text: Vault provides limited templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine, rather than functions for composing configuration values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Both features named in the claim exist in HashiCorp's docs. Username templating "uses the Go template language" to shape dynamic usernames in some secrets engines, and the Transform secrets engine encodes and decodes data (FPE, masking, tokenization). Calling this "limited" rather than a set of config-composition functions is a subjective characterization, but a reasonable one.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim leaves out client-side templating in Vault's ecosystem: Vault Agent templates (consul-template) and Vault Secrets Operator "advanced templating" can compose secret values into config files. A reviewer may want to add a qualifier.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide audit logs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Vault docs say "Audit devices are mountable devices that log requests and responses in Vault." Pulumi's ESC docs say "Audit logs enable you to track the activity of users within your ESC environments." Note: Vault turns auditing off by default until you enable an audit device, but it still provides audit logs.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The auto-generated Pulumi Cloud REST API reference says the ESC encrypt endpoint returns the definition with secret values "encrypted using the environment's encryption key", which supports per-environment keys at rest. The ESC CMK docs add that data keys are used to encrypt ESC secrets. I found no ESC-specific statement of TLS in transit, but Pulumi Cloud serves its API over HTTPS.
verdicts.framing_note: Per-environment key is backed by the API reference, which is generated from the product. The TLS half is backed only indirectly: general Pulumi Cloud HTTPS, with no ESC-specific source.

verdicts.text: Vault uses a security barrier for all requests to the backend, which automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit AES cipher in GCM mode with 96-bit nonces.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Vault Security Model page says: "Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend. The security barrier automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher in the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces." Vault's barrier_aes_gcm.go source backs this up: it uses a 256-bit key and Go's default 12-byte (96-bit) nonce.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is a near-word-for-word paraphrase of the official HashiCorp security model text. It only drops the word "made" and shortens "Advanced Encryption Standard" to "AES".

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide access controls.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say "Vault policies provide a declarative way to allow or deny access to certain paths and operations in Vault." The pulumi/esc repo says "Every environment can be locked down with RBAC, versioned, and audited." One caveat: Pulumi's own docs say ESC access controls and Teams are only available in the Enterprise and Business Critical editions.
verdicts.framing_note: This is a general statement that both products have a feature. Both vendors' sources confirm it. For ESC, the feature depends on which edition you have.

verdicts.text: Vault cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, and each engine is configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint them.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The first half is accurate: Vault's AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud secrets engines do issue short-lived credentials. The second half, that every engine is configured with a static credential, is wrong. HashiCorp's AWS API docs say "Credentials can be configured either with IAM access keys for a privileged AWS account, or using Plugin Workload Identity Federation (WIF)". WIF is available for the AWS, GCP, and Azure engines, and HashiCorp says it removes the need for static credentials. Separately, the AWS engine can also pick up credentials from the IAM/ECS instance it runs on.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Static root credentials are the default setup, and the only option in Community edition. WIF is Enterprise-only, so a narrower wording such as "typically configured with a static credential (unless using Enterprise WIF)" would be accurate.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and `pulumi-service` provider.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi docs confirm Pulumi Cloud/ESC acts as an OIDC issuer ("Pulumi ESC can be configured to act as an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider"). They also show OIDC being set up from the console UI, the CLI (`pulumi env setup`), and the pulumiservice provider (`DeploymentSettings` operationContext.oidc). I found no public source for the "Pulumi SDK" surface, and all the evidence comes from editorial pulumi.com pages.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Used as an OIDC provider from the SDK, CLI, UI, and pulumi-service provider" reads oddly. It may mix up "configured/managed from" with "used as a provider", and the SDK surface isn't clear.

verdicts.text: Configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Vault provider ships an `identity.OidcProvider` resource (`sdk/nodejs/identity/oidcProvider.ts`, alongside OIDC client/key/assignment resources). So you can configure Vault as an OIDC provider through infrastructure as code, not only from the CLI. Vault's HTTP API endpoint `/identity/oidc/provider` and its web UI likely also support this, but I did not fetch sources for them in this session.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Only available from the CLI" is a strong claim that looks wrong: Vault features are generally exposed through the HTTP API, and a Terraform/Pulumi resource for this exists.
